chapters.n: Paul introduces himself as an apostle called by God’s will, writing with Timothy. Paul had never visited Colosse; he writes from prison to a branch founded by his co-worker Epaphras.

f.g: One sent forth — a special witness of Christ.

chapters.n: He greets the faithful Saints in Colosse, a small city in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor (modern Turkey), near Laodicea and Hierapolis.

f.g: A town in the Roman province of Asia, about 100 miles east of Ephesus.
Holy ones — members set apart by covenant, not perfect people.

chapters.n: Paul and Timothy constantly thank God the Father for the Colossians in their prayers.
They are grateful because they have heard of the Colossians’ faith in Christ and their love for all fellow believers.
That faith and love grow out of hope — the reward stored up for them in heaven, which they learned about when the true gospel was first taught to them. Faith, hope, and love appear together.

f.w: hope which is laid up for you in heaven

chapters.n: The gospel is bearing fruit and growing all over the world, just as it has among them since they first understood God’s grace.
They learned the gospel from Epaphras, a beloved fellow servant who faithfully ministers to them on Christ’s behalf.
Epaphras has told Paul about the love the Spirit has kindled among them.

Ever since hearing this, Paul has prayed that they would be filled with knowledge of God’s will through wisdom and spiritual understanding. True knowledge, he hints, comes by the Spirit — not from the clever philosophies troubling Colosse.
The purpose of that knowledge is a life that pleases the Lord: bearing good fruit and coming to know God better and better.
Paul prays they will be strengthened by God’s glorious power — not to do spectacular things, but to endure patiently and joyfully.

f.g: Patience with people and hardship over a long time.

chapters.n: They should thank the Father, who has qualified them to share the inheritance of His holy people in the kingdom of light.
God has rescued us from darkness’s power and moved us into the kingdom of His beloved Son — like a whole people relocated to a new land.
In Christ we are redeemed — bought back — and our sins are forgiven through His blood.

f.g: Release by payment of a ransom.

chapters.n: Paul begins a majestic hymn about Christ: He is the perfect image of the unseen Father and the Firstborn, holding the highest rank over all creation. Latter-day Saints understand Him as the Firstborn spirit child of the Father.
Through Christ all things were created — in heaven and on earth, seen and unseen, including every heavenly rank and power. Everything was made by Him and for Him.

f.w: all things were created by him
thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers
f.g: Ranks of heavenly or spiritual beings; some at Colosse apparently worshipped such beings.

chapters.n: Christ existed before everything, and He holds all creation together.
He is also head of the Church, His body. As the first to rise from the dead, He holds first place in everything.
The Father chose to have His complete fulness live in the Son. Nothing of God is missing in Christ, so there is no need for other spiritual intermediaries.
Through Christ, and through the peace He made by His blood on the cross, God reconciles all things to Himself — on earth and in heaven.

f.g: Bring back into harmony and friendship.

chapters.n: You Colossians were once far from God, enemies in your thinking because of wicked deeds — yet now He has reconciled you.
He did this through His physical death, so that He can present you to God holy, spotless, and free from accusation.

f.g: His real physical body — answering any teaching that Christ only seemed human.

chapters.n: This is conditional: you must remain firm in the faith, grounded like a building on a foundation, not drifting from the hope of the gospel that Paul serves.
Paul rejoices in suffering for them. He sees his hardships as part of the afflictions Christ’s people must bear for the Church — not adding to Christ’s Atonement, but sharing in His work.
God gave Paul a stewardship to serve the Gentiles by fully preaching His word.
That word was a “mystery” — a truth hidden for ages but now revealed to the Saints. In scripture, a mystery is something known only by revelation.

f.g: A sacred truth known only through revelation, not a puzzle.

chapters.n: And the mystery is astonishing: Christ Himself dwells in Gentile believers, giving them the sure hope of glory.

f.w: Christ in you, the hope of glory

chapters.n: So Paul preaches Christ, warning and teaching everyone with wisdom, so he can present every person complete and mature in Christ.
To this end he works hard, struggling with all the energy that Christ powerfully works within him.

f.g: Greek agōnizomai — contending as in an athletic contest.

chapters.n: Paul wants them to know how hard he struggles in prayer and concern for them, for the nearby Saints at Laodicea, and for all believers who have never met him in person.
His goal is that their hearts be encouraged and woven together in love, leading to the rich, confident understanding of God’s revealed mystery — Christ Himself.

f.g: Joined together, as ligaments join a body.

chapters.n: All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are stored up in Christ. False teachers offered secret knowledge; Paul says it is all found in Him.
He says this so no one can trick them with smooth, persuasive arguments.
Though Paul is far away, he is with them in spirit and delights to see their good order and firm faith — like a commander pleased with disciplined troops.

f.g: Orderly ranks, discipline — a military term.

chapters.n: Since you received Christ as your Lord, keep living your daily life in Him.
Paul mixes images: be rooted in Christ like a tree, built up like a building, and firmly established in faith, overflowing with gratitude.
Watch out that no one carries you off as captives through empty philosophy and human traditions that are based on the world’s basic principles instead of on Christ.

f.g: Carry off as plunder, take captive.
Elementary principles; possibly spiritual forces thought to rule the cosmos.

chapters.n: In Christ the full nature of Deity lives in bodily form. He is not one spiritual being among many; He is fully divine and truly embodied.
And in Him you lack nothing. He is ruler over every spiritual power, so you don’t need angels or other powers to make you complete.
In Christ you received a spiritual circumcision, not done by human hands: the cutting away of your old sinful nature.
In baptism you were buried with Christ and raised with Him, through faith in God’s power that raised Him from the dead. Baptism by immersion symbolizes death, burial, and resurrection.
You were spiritually dead in sin, outside the covenant — yet God made you alive with Christ and forgave all your sins.

Christ canceled the written record of debt that stood against us — like an IOU — and nailed it to His cross. Executions sometimes posted the charge on the cross; here the charge against us is cancelled there.
On the cross Christ disarmed hostile spiritual powers and paraded them publicly as defeated, like a Roman general leading captives in a triumph.

f.w: made a shew of them openly
f.g: Displayed them publicly, as in a victory procession.

chapters.n: So don’t let anyone judge you over food and drink rules or the observance of festivals, new moons, or Sabbaths — practices from the law of Moses some were pressing on Gentile converts.
Those observances were a shadow pointing ahead to Christ; He is the reality that casts the shadow.

f.w: a shadow of things to come

chapters.n: Don’t let anyone cheat you out of your prize by showing off false humility, worshipping angels, and boasting about visions — people inflated by a worldly mind.

f.g: Disqualify you, as an umpire rules a runner out of the prize.

chapters.n: Such people have lost their connection to Christ, the Head. From Him the whole body, held together by joints and ligaments, grows as God makes it grow.
If you died with Christ to the world’s basic principles, why live as though you still belonged to the world, submitting to its rules?

f.g: Here, man-made regulations, not sacred priesthood ordinances.

chapters.n: Paul mocks the rules false teachers pushed: Don’t handle! Don’t taste! Don’t touch!

f.g: Probably strict purity rules about food and contact.

chapters.n: These rules concern things that are used up and gone, and they are based on human commandments and teachings, not God’s.
Such rules look wise, with their self-made religion, show of humility, and harsh treatment of the body — but they have no real power to restrain sinful desires.

f.g: Severe treatment of the body, asceticism.

chapters.n: Since you have been raised to new life with Christ (as baptism symbolizes), set your aims on heavenly things, where Christ reigns at the Father’s right hand.
Fix your mind and heart on heavenly things, not on earthly ones.
Your old self has died, and your true life is now safely hidden with Christ in God — protected, though not yet fully seen.

f.g: Kept secret and safe, like treasure.

chapters.n: When Christ — your very life — appears at His Second Coming, you will be revealed with Him in glory.
So put to death the earthly sins within you: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed — which is really a form of idol worship.
Because of these sins, God’s judgment comes on those who persist in disobedience.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for disobedient people.

chapters.n: You once lived that way yourselves, before the gospel changed you.
Now strip off these too, like dirty clothes: anger, rage, malice, slander, and obscene talk.

f.g: Here, slander or abusive speech against others.

chapters.n: Don’t lie to one another, since you have taken off your old self and its habits.
You have put on a new self, constantly being renewed in true knowledge to match the image of its Creator — becoming more like God.

f.w: image of him that created him

chapters.n: In this new life, ethnic, religious, cultural, and social barriers fall away. Christ is everything, and He is in everyone who believes.

f.g: Nomads north of the Black Sea, considered the most uncivilized people of the time.

chapters.n: As God’s chosen, holy, and beloved people, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience.
Bear with one another and forgive any grievance, just as Christ forgave you.
Over all these virtues, put on charity — Christlike love — which ties them together into a complete whole, like a belt over garments.

f.g: The bond that makes everything complete.

chapters.n: Let Christ’s peace act as umpire in your hearts, deciding between choices. You were called to be one body in peace — and be grateful.

f.g: Greek brabeuō — to umpire, to decide.

chapters.n: Let Christ’s words live richly in you. Teach and encourage each other through psalms, hymns, and sacred songs, singing to the Lord with gratitude.

f.w: psalms and hymns and spiritual songs

chapters.n: Whatever you say or do, do it all in Jesus’s name, thanking the Father through Him.

f.w: in the name of the Lord Jesus

chapters.n: Paul now gives guidance for households, as Roman society expected. Wives are to support their husbands in a way that fits life in the Lord — a key qualifier.

f.w: as it is fit in the Lord
f.g: Within what is proper for disciples of Christ.

chapters.n: Husbands must love their wives and never be harsh or bitter toward them — a strong call in a culture that gave husbands great power.
Children should obey their parents, which pleases the Lord.
Fathers must not exasperate or nag their children, or the children will lose heart.
Many early Christians were slaves. Paul tells them to serve sincerely, not just when the master is watching or to win favor, but with an undivided heart, reverencing God.
Whatever your work, do it wholeheartedly, as if working for the Lord rather than for people.
The Lord Himself will repay you with an inheritance — something slaves could not legally receive in Rome. Your real master is Christ.
And whoever does wrong — master or servant — will be repaid for it. God shows no favoritism.
Masters must treat their servants justly and fairly, remembering that they too answer to a Master in heaven. This verse finishes the household instructions of chapter 3.
Keep praying faithfully, staying alert and thankful as you pray.
Pray for us too, Paul asks — that God will open doors for preaching the message of Christ, the very message that put him in chains.
And pray that he will explain it clearly, as he should.
Act wisely toward people outside the Church, making the most of every opportunity.
Let your conversation always be gracious and “seasoned with salt” — interesting, wholesome, and wise — so you know how to answer each person.
Tychicus, a beloved and faithful co-worker, will tell them all about Paul’s situation. He likely carried this letter (and Ephesians) to Asia.
Paul sends him specifically to learn how they are doing and encourage them.
Onesimus travels with him — the runaway slave from Colosse who became a believer. Paul now calls him “faithful and beloved,” “one of you.” His story is told in Philemon.
Paul sends greetings from Aristarchus, a fellow prisoner, and from Mark, Barnabas’s cousin. Mark had once left Paul’s mission, but here he is fully restored to Paul’s trust.
Jesus Justus also greets them. These three were the only Jewish Christians working with Paul at the time, and they have been a real comfort.

f.g: “Jesus” (Joshua) was a common Jewish name; he used the Latin surname Justus.

chapters.n: Epaphras, their own founder and teacher, sends greetings. He is always wrestling in prayer for them to stand mature and fully assured in God’s will.
Paul vouches for Epaphras’s deep concern for the Saints in all three Lycus valley cities.

f.g: A city about six miles north of Laodicea, known for hot springs.

chapters.n: Luke, the beloved doctor and author of Luke and Acts, greets them, as does Demas — who later abandoned Paul.
Paul greets the Saints in Laodicea, and Nymphas and the congregation meeting in that home. Early branches gathered in members’ houses.

f.w: the church which is in his house

chapters.n: Paul wants his letters shared between branches. The “epistle from Laodicea” is apparently a letter of Paul’s that has not survived — evidence that not all inspired writings are in the Bible.

f.g: A lost letter; some think it may be Ephesians, but it is unknown.

chapters.n: A personal note to Archippus: be sure to complete the ministry the Lord gave you.
Paul usually dictated letters to a scribe but signed the greeting in his own hand. “Remember my bonds” — don’t forget I am in chains — is his final request.

f.w: by the hand of me Paul
